difficultyReason: Conclusion rests on two conjoined conditions — professional role plus public interest. Trap (B) is too broad; it would license a conclusion even when no public interest is at stake. Trap (D) is too narrow, applying only to physicians.
stimulus: Ethicist: A pharmacist who fills prescriptions at a neighborhood clinic learned that a widely used heartburn medication was being recalled for contamination. The manufacturer had asked pharmacies to delay informing patients until a formal press release could be issued. The pharmacist nonetheless called every affected patient that day. Given that the contamination posed a genuine risk of harm, the pharmacist acted rightly in doing so.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A health-care professional who learns of a material risk to the people under her care is obligated to inform them promptly, even when instructed otherwise by third parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who receives confidential information from an employer is permitted to disclose that information whenever she believes disclosure would be beneficial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients are entitled to complete information about every medication they have ever been prescribed, regardless of current relevance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician who has prescribed a medication later found to be unsafe must personally contact each patient who received the prescription.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Manufacturers of pharmaceuticals bear primary responsibility for communicating safety information to the public.

explanations.correct: The ethicist concludes the pharmacist acted rightly because (i) she is a health-care professional, (ii) a real risk of harm existed, and (iii) a third party asked her to delay. Principle (A) combines these exact conditions and yields the endorsement.
explanations.B: Too broad — permits any employee to disclose confidential information on a mere belief that disclosure is beneficial, licensing conclusions the ethicist does not draw.
explanations.C: Too broad and tangential — it concerns completeness of medication histories, not acute safety risks.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the actor in the stimulus is a pharmacist, not a physician, so the principle would not cover this case.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject to manufacturer responsibility, which is not what the ethicist is defending.

difficultyReason: Argument depends on both foreseeability and counterfactual avoidability. Trap (C) inverts the direction; trap (E) applies only to intentional harm.
stimulus: Columnist: The city's transit agency continued to run its oldest subway cars for two years after internal engineers reported that a brake component was prone to failure at high speed. A derailment last month, caused by precisely that component, injured dozens of riders. The agency's leadership argues that the derailment was a freak accident for which no one is to blame. That defense fails: the agency is culpable for the harm.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An organization is culpable for a harm when it has been warned of a specific risk and continues a practice that could have been altered to prevent that harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An organization is culpable for a harm only if its leadership directly intended the harmful outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An organization that cannot rule out every possible mechanical failure must cease operations until its equipment is certified safe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public agencies bear a heavier duty of care than private firms performing comparable services.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one is to blame for harms that arise from accidents the responsible parties did not foresee.

explanations.correct: The columnist stresses (i) the agency was warned of this specific brake risk and (ii) could have withdrawn the cars but did not. Principle (A) combines warning plus avoidability to yield culpability — exactly the move the columnist makes.
explanations.B: Too narrow — would acquit the agency in this case, since intent is not alleged.
explanations.C: Too broad — would license halting operations in any case of residual uncertainty, a conclusion the columnist does not draw.
explanations.D: Tangential — comparison of public versus private duty is not what the columnist is defending.
explanations.E: Addresses a different aspect — defines when no one is to blame, not when culpability attaches; and the stimulus shows the risk was foreseen.

difficultyReason: Requires a principle matching both the consent gap and the material-effect condition in the researcher's critique. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (D) is reversed.
stimulus: Researcher: A recent linguistic study recorded casual conversations in public cafés to document regional slang, informing only the café owners and not the patrons being recorded. The investigators claim that because no names were published, no harm was done. But patrons could be identified by voice in the audio files released with the paper, and several later reported embarrassment when colleagues recognized them. The study's method was ethically indefensible.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the researcher's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Researchers must secure informed consent from participants whenever the research materials released could reasonably be used to identify them and affect their standing with others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All social-science research involving human subjects must obtain written consent from every subject before any data collection begins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Research is ethically defensible only when its scientific value clearly outweighs any inconvenience to the subjects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants need not consent to research so long as their personal names are withheld from publication.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public spaces afford no expectation of privacy, and research conducted in them is therefore exempt from consent requirements.

explanations.correct: The researcher's complaint rests on two facts: patrons were identifiable from the released audio, and that identification produced real social harm. Principle (A) joins identifiability and adverse standing into a consent requirement, licensing the 'ethically indefensible' verdict.
explanations.B: Too broad — a blanket written-consent rule would condemn studies the researcher is not condemning and ignores the identifiability criterion she actually invokes.
explanations.C: Tangential — cost-benefit weighing is not the basis of the researcher's critique.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would exonerate the investigators, since names were indeed withheld.
explanations.E: Reversed — would license the study's design rather than condemn it.

difficultyReason: Conclusion blames a regulator on grounds of available knowledge plus preventable magnitude. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (E) shifts the subject to industry.
stimulus: Economist: The financial regulator had ample data showing that a particular class of mortgage-backed securities was badly mispriced, and it had the statutory authority to require banks to mark these holdings down. Choosing not to act, the regulator allowed losses to mount until several mid-sized banks failed, costing taxpayers billions. The regulator is properly faulted for the scope of those losses.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A public official is to blame for any adverse outcome occurring within the sphere of that official's authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A regulator who possesses both the evidence of a growing harm and the authority to mitigate it is properly faulted for the portion of the harm that its inaction allowed to continue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Financial regulators ought to privilege market stability over the enforcement of individual accounting rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Private firms, not public regulators, bear ultimate responsibility for the soundness of their own balance sheets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Industries whose failures impose large costs on taxpayers should face stricter oversight than industries whose failures do not.

explanations.correct: The economist faults the regulator on two specific grounds: it had the data (evidence) and the authority (power to mitigate), and its inaction allowed additional harm. Principle (B) joins these exact conditions to fault.
explanations.A: Too broad — would fault the regulator even when it lacked relevant evidence or lawful tools, licensing conclusions stronger than the economist's.
explanations.C: Tangential — the economist is not making a claim about how to rank stability against accounting rules.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle shifts blame away from the regulator the economist is faulting.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject from regulator conduct to the design of oversight regimes generally.

difficultyReason: Judgment depends jointly on genuine effort and on outcome-independent acknowledgment. Trap (C) is too narrow to primary caregivers; trap (E) is reversed.
stimulus: Teacher: Priya spent weeks tutoring a younger student in algebra, preparing customized worksheets and meeting twice a week even during exam season. The younger student's grades did not substantially improve, and the school's tutoring coordinator argues that Priya therefore deserves no recognition. The coordinator is mistaken: Priya deserves recognition for her tutoring work.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the teacher's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who volunteers to assist another student deserves formal recognition from the school, whatever their methods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who devotes sustained and conscientious effort to helping another deserves recognition for that effort, whether or not the effort produces its intended outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary caregivers and teachers who guide a child's long-term development deserve public acknowledgment for that guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recognition should be reserved for students whose assistance measurably improves the academic performance of those they help.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tutors should be evaluated primarily on the test-score gains of the students they tutor.

explanations.correct: The teacher endorses recognition because Priya expended genuine, sustained effort, and does so despite the absence of a measurable outcome. Principle (B) joins effort-and-conscientiousness to recognition and explicitly decouples it from outcomes.
explanations.A: Too broad — 'whatever their methods' licenses recognition for haphazard or counterproductive efforts the teacher is not endorsing.
explanations.C: Too narrow — Priya is a peer tutor, not a primary caregiver, so the principle does not cover her case.
explanations.D: Reversed — would deny Priya recognition, since grades did not improve.
explanations.E: Reversed — endorses the coordinator's view, not the teacher's.

difficultyReason: Preservation judgment rests on two linked criteria — historical function and irreplaceability. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (D) is reversed.
stimulus: Preservationist: The nineteenth-century glass conservatory in Marston Park is structurally unsound and would cost nearly as much to restore as to demolish and replace. The parks department therefore favors demolition. But the conservatory is the only surviving example of a glazing technique once central to the city's industrial identity, a technique no living craftsperson can fully reconstruct. The parks department should restore, not demolish, the conservatory.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the preservationist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a structure is both a unique surviving exemplar of a historically significant technique and cannot be reconstructed using contemporary methods, it should be restored rather than demolished.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All structures more than a century old should be preserved whenever doing so is physically possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public parks should allocate funds equally between new construction and the maintenance of existing structures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When restoration and replacement costs are comparable, a municipality should choose whichever option yields greater future utility for visitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cities have a duty to commemorate their industrial heritage through public monuments and explanatory plaques.

explanations.correct: The preservationist's conclusion rests on (i) the conservatory's uniqueness as a surviving exemplar of the glazing technique and (ii) the technique's non-reconstructibility today. Principle (A) joins those exact conditions to a restoration duty.
explanations.B: Too broad — a blanket century-old rule would mandate preservation in many cases the preservationist does not discuss and ignores uniqueness and reconstructibility.
explanations.C: Tangential — budget allocation policy doesn't speak to this specific demolish-or-restore choice.
explanations.D: Reversed — future-utility weighing could favor demolition-plus-replacement and would not license the preservationist's conclusion.
explanations.E: Tangential — plaques and monuments are a different preservation strategy than structural restoration.

difficultyReason: Verdict requires both the content-creator relationship and the commercial-use condition. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (E) is too narrow.
stimulus: Critic: A regional museum scanned three hundred paintings by local artists to generate an interactive exhibit, then licensed the same scans to a textile company that printed the images on scarves sold at a substantial profit. The artists, most of whom had donated the originals for exhibition purposes, received nothing. The museum's decision to license the scans for commercial resale was wrong.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An institution that acquires any work of art acquires along with it the right to use the work in any manner the institution sees fit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An institution that obtains works from their creators for a specified noncommercial purpose acts wrongly in subsequently licensing those works for commercial profit without the creators' involvement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums should prioritize public access to artworks over the financial interests of the artists who created them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digital reproductions of artworks must be identified as reproductions whenever they are displayed to the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum that sells original paintings it owns outright must share the proceeds with the living artists who painted them.

explanations.correct: The critic's verdict rests on two facts: the artists transferred the works for a specific noncommercial purpose (exhibition), and the museum then licensed them for commercial profit without the artists. Principle (B) joins those conditions to wrongdoing.
explanations.C: Tangential — access-versus-income is not the axis of the critic's complaint, which is about scope of use.
explanations.D: Tangential — labeling reproductions is a different issue.
explanations.E: Too narrow — addresses sale of original paintings, not licensing of digital scans, and so would not cover the case at hand.

difficultyReason: Conclusion rests on both disproportionate burden and availability of less restrictive means. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (D) is too narrow.
stimulus: Policy analyst: The state's new rule requires anyone wishing to braid hair professionally to complete 1,500 hours of cosmetology training and pass a chemistry exam covering dyes the braiders never use. The rule is meant to protect consumers from unsanitary practices, but the same safety outcome could be achieved through a short sanitation course and a simple inspection regime. The state's rule is unjustified.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the policy analyst's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government regulation is unjustified unless it is supported by a majority of the workers in the regulated trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government regulation that imposes significant burdens on those it regulates is unjustified when a substantially less burdensome alternative would achieve the same legitimate purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumer-protection regulations should be tailored to the specific risks of each trade rather than modeled on unrelated trades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occupational licensing requirements for hair braiders must exclude material on chemical hair dyes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any regulation motivated by a legitimate safety interest is justified regardless of the costs it imposes on workers.

explanations.correct: The analyst's verdict rests on (i) the rule's heavy burden on braiders and (ii) the availability of a much less burdensome alternative that achieves the same safety aim. Principle (B) joins those exact conditions to an unjustified verdict.
explanations.A: Too broad and off-point — would condemn many rules regardless of whether less burdensome alternatives exist, and majority approval is not the analyst's criterion.
explanations.C: Tangential — captures a related intuition (tailoring) but does not join burden and least-restrictive-means, which are the analyst's actual grounds.
explanations.D: Too narrow — a rule about hair-dye content on licensing exams would justify only part of the analyst's critique, leaving the 1,500-hour burden unaddressed.
explanations.E: Reversed — would license the rule, not condemn it.

difficultyReason: Entitlement depends on both the voluntary disclosure and the absence of countervailing third-party harm. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (E) is reversed.
stimulus: Librarian: A patron who checked out several books on computer security asked the library to delete his borrowing records for the past year, citing concerns that an employer-conducted background check might misread them. The library's records contain no information about anyone other than the patron himself, and erasing them would compromise no other patron's interests. The library should honor the request.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the librarian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An institution should, upon the voluntary request of the person to whom records exclusively pertain, erase those records whenever doing so harms no one else's legitimate interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Libraries should accede to any patron request that does not violate state or federal law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Institutions should retain borrowing records indefinitely so that patterns of misuse can be detected retrospectively.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An individual's reading history is among the most sensitive categories of personal information and deserves the highest level of legal protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employers performing background checks are entitled to access library borrowing records that would otherwise be confidential.

explanations.correct: The librarian's conclusion rests on (i) the patron's own voluntary request about records that pertain only to him and (ii) the absence of harm to others' interests. Principle (A) combines both conditions to yield erasure.
explanations.B: Too broad — 'any request that doesn't violate law' would license many requests the librarian does not endorse and ignores the harm-to-others condition she relies on.
explanations.D: Tangential — a claim about legal status of reading history does not license erasure in this particular case.
explanations.E: Reversed and tangential — authorizes disclosure to employers rather than erasure for the patron.

difficultyReason: Permission depends on reversibility joined with lack of viable alternatives. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (D) is tangential.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Some ecologists object to the release of genetically modified mosquitoes engineered to suppress populations carrying a deadly fever, worrying that releases could disrupt local ecosystems. In the island region under discussion, however, the engineered mosquitoes' modifications fade within a few generations if releases are halted, and no other method has reduced the fever there despite decades of effort. Releasing the engineered mosquitoes in this region is permissible.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmental scientist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that may save human lives from a deadly disease is permissible regardless of its ecological consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An ecological intervention addressing a serious public-health threat is permissible when its effects can be halted and no established alternative has proven effective in the affected region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific research involving genetic modification must first be tested in contained laboratory settings before any field deployment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regions affected by a mosquito-borne disease should adopt the intervention proven most effective in other regions with comparable climates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Once an ecological intervention has shown any adverse effect in a pilot trial, it should not be expanded to wider release.

explanations.correct: The scientist's permission rests on two joined facts: the intervention is reversible (modifications fade) and alternatives have long failed in this region. Principle (B) combines serious threat, reversibility, and lack of proven alternatives, licensing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Too broad — ignores ecological consequences entirely and would license interventions the scientist is not endorsing.
explanations.C: Tangential — contained-lab testing is not the question; the stimulus concerns a field release already past that stage.
explanations.D: Tangential — the scientist's argument hinges on this region's failure history and on reversibility, not on transplanting methods from other regions.
